item.title: America's Covid Fraud Totals Over $300B
item.description: The author counts likely fraud across federal and state pandemic programs at over three hundred billion dollars, mostly in small business loans and unemployment benefits. The piece argues this follows from policy choices that skipped verification and rewarded spending over prevention, and that little has been recovered. Music: “Hop” by Monplaisir (CC0).

item.title: My California Ballot, 2026
item.description: Scott Alexander walks through how he is voting in Oakland, California, on state propositions, state officials, local measures and local races, with his reasoning on each. He ends by testing whether an AI could have predicted his votes, and finds it only got fifty-seven percent right. Music: “Hop” by Monplaisir (CC0).

item.title: Neural Networks Are Already Clean
item.description: Nick Cammarata argues that apparent polysemanticity in neural networks is mostly recursive generalization rather than superposition, so a network's own neurons and circuits can be studied directly. He supports this with vision and language model experiments and argues for exploratory, agent-driven interpretability. item.title: What's the ROI of software engineers' spending on AI?
item.description: The author surveyed engineering leaders at twenty-seven companies, plus data from CodeRabbit and Gitar, to see what companies spend on AI per engineer and how pull request throughput changed. Spending varies widely and is unrelated to company size, and gains in throughput are uneven, with return on investment hard to pin down. item.title: Evaluating how AI agents use tools
item.description: AgentMail tested twenty-five model-and-harness agents on seven email tasks and found that agents rarely fail at the work itself, but at points where the tool leaves them guessing, such as hidden filtered mail, misleadingly named endpoints, and ambiguous spam labels. Most fixes belong to the tool: say what was filtered, name operations for what they do, and explain what labels mean. Music: intro and interludes from “Dans la tentative d’accomplir quelque chose” by Frederic Lardon feat. Laura Palmée (CC0). Outro: “Crap Transition” by Jesse Spillane, https://freemusicarchive.org/music/Jesse_Spillane/Art_of_Presentation/Jesse_Spillane_-_Art_of_Presentation_-_04_Crap_Transition/ licensed CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); trimmed, faded and mixed with narration.

item.title: Single points of failure in military AI command
item.description: As autonomous systems replace human soldiers and officers, control of a military can collapse toward a single point of failure at the top. Nuclear command-and-control offers three kinds of safeguards, integrity, containment and soundness of command, but the ones that constrain the top are the least likely to be adopted. item.description: A father describes how a chatbot playing a TV doctor suggested the MRI that found a fibroid behind his wife's six years of unexplained infertility, leading to a natural pregnancy after surgery. He uses the story to argue that AI's everyday benefits deserve acknowledgment alongside its risks. Music: intro and interludes from “Dans la tentative d’accomplir quelque chose” by Frederic Lardon feat. Laura Palmée (CC0). item.title: Can AI automate AI R&D yet?
item.description: Using an evaluation called InnovationEval, the piece tests whether frontier AI models can independently rediscover a recent machine learning innovation, and finds they fall far short, reaching at most fifteen percent of the original gains while overstating their results. Progress is fast, so the authors plan to repeat the test on newer models. Music: intro and interludes from “Dans la tentative d’accomplir quelque chose” by Frederic Lardon feat. Laura Palmée (CC0). Outro: “Crap Transition” by Jesse Spillane, https://freemusicarchive.org/music/Jesse_Spillane/Art_of_Presentation/Jesse_Spillane_-_Art_of_Presentation_-_04_Crap_Transition/ licensed CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); trimmed, faded and mixed with narration.

item.title: Current AIs out-persuade professionals in lab settings but (probably) not in the world
item.description: The author argues that experiments show AIs beating professional humans at narrow persuasion tasks, but real-world evidence suggests broad AI persuasion sits between median human and median professional level. item.title: The Bitter Lesson
item.description: Looking back over decades of AI research, the piece argues that general methods which scale with computation, namely search and learning, have always eventually beaten approaches that build in human knowledge, and that researchers should build meta-methods that discover rather than encode what we think we know. Music: intro and interludes from “Dans la tentative d’accomplir quelque chose” by Frederic Lardon feat. Laura Palmée (CC0).
